card.title: Clocks that flew around the world

panels.text: Relativity predicts that clocks run at slightly different rates depending on how they move and how strong gravity is. But can you measure it with an airliner?
In 1971 physicist Joseph Hafele and astronomer Richard Keating took four cesium atomic clocks on commercial flights twice around the world, first east, then west.
They compared the travelling clocks with clocks that stayed at the US Naval Observatory. When reunited, the clocks disagreed.
Measured against the ground clocks, the eastward clocks lost about 59 nanoseconds and the westward ones gained about 273. Relativity had predicted about -40 and +275, within the margin of error.

probes.question: What did the clocks show when they were reunited?

claims.claim: In 1971 Hafele (physicist) and Keating (astronomer) took four cesium atomic clocks on commercial flights twice around the world, east then west
claims.quote: took four cesium -beam atomic clocks aboard commercial airliners. They flew twice around the world, first eastward, then westward

claims.claim: They compared travelling clocks with stationary clocks at the US Naval Observatory
claims.quote: and compared the clocks in motion to stationary clocks at the United States Naval Observatory .

claims.claim: Clocks disagreed, in line with relativity's predictions (probe 1)
claims.quote: their differences were consistent with the predictions of special and general relativity .

claims.claim: Eastward measured about -59 ns, westward about +273; predicted about -40 and +275
claims.note: Table columns: predicted total then measured; eastward -40 predicted / -59 measured, westward +275 predicted / +273 measured.

claims.claim: Agreement within the margin of error
claims.quote: The observed time gains and losses were in agreement with relativistic predictions to within the ~10% precision expected of the experiment.

claims.claim: Relativity predicts clock rates depend on motion and gravity (altitude)
claims.quote: General relativity predicts an additional effect, in which an increase in gravitational potential due to altitude speeds the clocks up.
